headline: The American Hospital Association has disputed an insurer group's claim that hospitals' AI documentation tools are driving up health costs.
score_reason: Pool 5 kept: a trade-group rebuttal that adds the hospitals' side to a cost claim we carried, but it is an argument, not new data.
importance_line: Patients and the employers and insurers who pay for their care now have two competing accounts of whether AI documentation tools raise hospital bills, but both come from interested trade groups, and the AHA's reply is an argument rather than a review of patient records.
summary: The American Hospital Association (AHA), the US hospitals' trade group, said in a blog on 5 Oct 2026 that an analysis by the insurers' trade group, the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA), does not show that hospitals coded patients wrongly or that AI tools drive inappropriate spending. That analysis, carried in our 25 and 27 Sep 2026 editions, said coding changes linked to hospitals' AI documentation tools added $942 million to its plans' spending between 2023 and 2025; the AHA says it did not review medical records, does not appear to identify which claims involved AI, and may reflect older, sicker patients being documented more fully.
notes: Reply story: the AHA answers the BCBSA analysis carried in our 25 Sep 2026 (item 122) and 27 Sep 2026 (item 114) editions; the earlier edition said no hospital response was given. Full blog read; the pool link is the short AHA news item (https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2026-10-05-aha-blog-responds-bcbs-report-suggesting-hospitals-use-ai-documentation-tools-drives-increased). The BCBSA paper itself was not read.
